levelNote: Fifty foundational recall questions across Spenser, Sidney, Marlowe, Kyd, the University Wits, Shakespeare, the playhouses and the critics.

questions.question: Which years mark the beginning and end of the reign of Queen Elizabeth I over England?
questions.explanation: Queen Elizabeth I ascended the English throne in 1558 upon the death of Mary I and reigned until her death in 1603, when she was succeeded by James I.
questions.src: user-supplied: Upkar's UGC NET/JRF/SET English

questions.question: In which year were the first permanent public playhouses in London erected outside the city walls?
questions.explanation: After the London authorities drove public players beyond the city walls in 1575, the first permanent London public playhouses were built in 1576.
questions.src: user-supplied: Upkar's UGC NET/JRF/SET English

questions.question: In which year was the famous Globe Theatre built on Bankside in London by William Shakespeare's playing company?
questions.explanation: The Globe Theatre, the most famous playhouse of the Elizabethan Age and home to the Lord Chamberlain's Men, was built in 1599.
questions.src: user-supplied: Upkar's UGC NET/JRF/SET English

questions.question: To which London acting company—renamed the King's Men after the accession of James I in 1603—did William Shakespeare belong as actor, playwright, and shareholder?
questions.explanation: During Elizabeth's reign, William Shakespeare was an actor, playwright, and part-owner (sharer) in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, which became the King's Men under James I.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which major Elizabethan theatrical company staged the plays of Christopher Marlowe?
questions.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's great tragedies were performed by the Lord Admiral's Men, the chief rival company to the Lord Chamberlain's Men.
questions.src: user-supplied: Easy Handbook for NET English Literature

questions.question: At which indoor London theatre were John Lyly's court comedies performed by the boy companies known as the Children of the Chapel and the Children of Paul's?
questions.explanation: In 1583 John Lyly gained control of the first Blackfriars Theatre, where his prose comedies were acted by the Children of the Chapel and the Children of Paul's.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: At which Elizabethan playhouse managed by Philip Henslowe was Thomas Kyd's revenge play The Spanish Tragedy staged in 1592?
questions.explanation: Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy was staged at The Rose Theatre for the theatrical entrepreneur Philip Henslowe in 1592 and later performed at the Swan Theatre in 1597.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In which Warwickshire market town on the River Avon was William Shakespeare born in April 1564?
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare was born in April 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, to John Shakespeare and Mary Arden, earning him the title 'the Bard of Avon'.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: At which 1586 battle in the Netherlands was Sir Philip Sidney mortally wounded in the thigh?
questions.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney (1554–1586) was mortally wounded in the thigh while fighting the Spanish at the Battle of Zutphen in 1586 and died within a month.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question:
Arrange the following milestones of the Elizabethan Age in chronological order:
(A) Accession of Queen Elizabeth I to the English throne
(B) Building of the first permanent London playhouses
(C) First performance of Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great
(D) Building of the Globe Theatre in London
questions.explanation: Queen Elizabeth I ascended the throne in 1558 (A); the first London playhouses were built in 1576 (B); Marlowe's Tamburlaine was staged in 1587 (C); and the Globe Theatre was built in 1599 (D).
questions.src: user-supplied: Upkar's UGC NET/JRF/SET English

questions.question: Who is the overall hero of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene, representing 'Magnificence' (the perfection of all the moral virtues) who seeks the Faerie Queene Gloriana?
questions.explanation: In Spenser's The Faerie Queene, Prince Arthur represents Magnificence—the sum and perfection of all the twelve virtues—and appears across the books to aid the individual knights while seeking Gloriana (Queen Elizabeth).
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which 1596 spousal poem by Edmund Spenser—containing the refrain 'Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song'—celebrates the double marriage of the two daughters of the Earl of Worcester?
questions.explanation: Spenser wrote Prothalamion (1596) as a spousal song celebrating the twin marriage of Lady Elizabeth Somerset and Lady Katherine Somerset, daughters of the Earl of Worcester; its famous refrain was later echoed by T. S. Eliot in The Waste Land.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which pastoral elegy did Edmund Spenser write (published in 1595 alongside Colin Clouts Come Home Againe) to mourn the death of Sir Philip Sidney?
questions.explanation: Edmund Spenser wrote the pastoral elegy Astrophel (published in 1595 and dedicated to Sidney's widow, the Countess of Essex) to mourn the death of his friend and patron Sir Philip Sidney.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: To which Elizabethan courtier, explorer, and fellow Irish landlord did Edmund Spenser dedicate his autobiographical pastoral poem Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595) as well as the prefatory letter to The Faerie Queene?
questions.explanation: Spenser addressed the 1590 prefatory letter of The Faerie Queene to Sir Walter Raleigh ('the Shepherd of the Ocean') and dedicated Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), recounting their 1591 visit to London, to Raleigh.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: How many sonnets and songs are contained in Sir Philip Sidney's Elizabethan sonnet sequence Astrophil and Stella?
questions.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney's Astrophil and Stella, the first great Elizabethan sonnet sequence (composed in the early 1580s, first printed in 1591), consists of 108 sonnets and 11 songs.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which famous Elizabethan pastoral lyric by Christopher Marlowe opens with the invitation 'Come live with me and be my love, / And we will all the pleasures prove'?
options: 'Weep Not, My Wanton, Smile upon My Knee'
'His Golden Locks Time Hath to Silver Turned'
questions.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's pastoral lyric 'The Passionate Shepherd to His Love' opens with the famous line 'Come live with me and be my love', which was later answered by Sir Walter Raleigh and quoted by Shakespeare in The Merry Wives of Windsor.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which 1593 mythological narrative poem—written in six-line iambic pentameter stanzas (ababcc) and dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton—was the first work published under William Shakespeare's name?
questions.explanation: Printed by Richard Field in 1593 and dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, third Earl of Southampton, Venus and Adonis (written in the six-line ababcc stanza) was the first work published under Shakespeare's name.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In which seven-line stanza form did William Shakespeare compose his tragic narrative poem The Rape of Lucrece, also dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare's tragic narrative poem The Rape of Lucrece, recounting the assault on the Roman matron Lucretia by Tarquin, is written in seven-line rhyme-royal stanzas and dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In William Shakespeare's 1609 Quarto of 154 Sonnets, what collective name is given to the opening group of Sonnets 1 to 17 ('From fairest creatures we desire increase'), which urge a young man to marry and father children?
questions.explanation: Sonnets 1–17 of Shakespeare's 154 sonnets are known as the 'Procreation Sonnets' because they urge the Fair Youth to marry and preserve his beauty through offspring; Sonnets 1–126 are addressed to the Fair Youth and Sonnets 127–152 to the Dark Lady.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question:
Which of the following 1590s sonnet sequences and their authors are correctly paired?
(A) Samuel Daniel — Delia (1592)
(B) Henry Constable — Diana (1592)
(C) Michael Drayton — Idea's Mirror (1594) and Thomas Lodge — Phillis (1593)
(D) Stephen Gosson — Amoretti (1595)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation: During the 1590s Elizabethan sonnet vogue sparked by Sidney's Astrophil and Stella (printed 1591), Samuel Daniel published Delia (1592), Henry Constable published Diana (1592), Thomas Lodge published Phillis (1593), and Michael Drayton published Idea's Mirror. Statement (D) is false because Amoretti (1595) was written by Edmund Spenser.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great (1587), who is the daughter of the Egyptian Sultan whom the Scythian shepherd-conqueror Tamburlaine captures, woos, and crowns Empress of Persia?
questions.explanation: In Part I of Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great (1587), Tamburlaine captures and falls in love with Zenocrate, daughter of the Sultan of Egypt, spares her father at her plea, and marries her at the close of Part I.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, what Latin warning mysteriously appears in congealed blood on Faustus's arm as he signs the deed selling his soul to Lucifer?
questions.explanation: When Doctor Faustus stabs his arm to sign the compact with Lucifer in his own blood, his blood congeals and the Latin warning 'Homo fuge' ('Fly, man!') appears inscribed on his arm.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, whose murder in the arbour drives his father Hieronimo, Knight Marshal of Spain, and his beloved Bel-Imperia to plot their bloody revenge?
questions.explanation: In Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, Lorenzo and the Portuguese prince Balthazar murder Hieronimo's son Don Horatio and hang his body in the arbour; Hieronimo and Bel-Imperia avenge Horatio during the play-within-a-play Soliman and Perseda.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In John Lyly's allegorical court comedy Endymion, the Man in the Moon (1591), which moon goddess—representing Queen Elizabeth I—awakens the sleeping Endymion with a kiss?
questions.explanation: In John Lyly's court comedy Endymion, the Man in the Moon (1591), Endymion loves the chaste moon goddess Cynthia (an allegorical compliment to Queen Elizabeth I), whose kiss finally wakes him from his forty-year enchanted sleep.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which early farcical play by William Shakespeare—featuring the twin masters Antipholus of Syracuse and Antipholus of Ephesus and their twin servants named Dromio—is the shortest of all Shakespeare's plays?
questions.explanation: The Comedy of Errors, revolving around two pairs of identical twins (the brothers Antipholus and their servants Dromio) separated in a shipwreck and reunited in Ephesus, is Shakespeare's shortest play.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, which mischievous fairy spirit—also called Robin Goodfellow—serves King Oberon and anoints the eyes of the sleeping lovers and Titania with magic flower juice?
questions.explanation: In A Midsummer Night's Dream (1595), Puck (or Robin Goodfellow) is King Oberon's jester and spirit who fetches the love-in-idleness flower and mistakenly applies its juice to Lysander's eyes as well as to Queen Titania's.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, which of the three caskets at Belmont—inscribed 'Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath'—does Bassanio select to win Portia's hand?
questions.explanation: In the casket test devised by Portia's father at Belmont in The Merchant of Venice, the Prince of Morocco chooses gold, the Prince of Arragon chooses silver, and Bassanio rightly chooses the humble lead casket.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Act II, Scene vii of Shakespeare's As You Like It, which melancholic lord in the Forest of Arden delivers the famous monologue beginning 'All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players'?
questions.explanation: In Act II, Scene vii of As You Like It (1599), the melancholic lord Jaques delivers the 'Seven Ages of Man' speech ('All the world's a stage') to Duke Senior and his companions in the Forest of Arden.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which comedy by William Shakespeare opens with Duke Orsino's famous lines on music and love: 'If music be the food of love, play on; / Give me excess of it'?
options: Twelfth Night, or What You Will
questions.explanation: Duke Orsino of Illyria speaks the opening lines 'If music be the food of love, play on' at the beginning of Act I, Scene i of Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question:
Match List I (Shakespearean Play) with List II (Central Pair of Lovers or Antagonists):

List I (Shakespearean Play)
(A) The Taming of the Shrew
(B) Much Ado About Nothing
(C) Romeo and Juliet
(D) Henry IV, Part 1

List II (Central Pair of Lovers or Antagonists)
(I) Beatrice and Benedick (in Messina)
(II) Petruchio and Katherine (in Padua)
(III) Prince Hal and Henry Percy, called Hotspur (at Shrewsbury)
(IV) The feuding houses of Montague and Capulet (in Verona)
questions.explanation: In The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio weds Katherine (A-II); in Much Ado About Nothing, Beatrice and Benedick exchange wit in Messina (B-I); Romeo and Juliet involves the Montague–Capulet feud (C-IV); and Henry IV, Part 1 culminates in Prince Hal's duel with Hotspur (D-III).
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which 1580 prose work did John Lyly publish as the direct sequel to Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578)?
options: Menaphon: Camilla's Alarum to Slumbering Euphues
questions.explanation: John Lyly followed Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578) with its sequel Euphues and His England (1580), narrating the voyage and adventures of Euphues and Philautus in England.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: In Book I of Sir Philip Sidney's pastoral prose romance Arcadia, who is the Duke of Arcadia whose wife is Gynecia and whose two daughters are Pamela and Philoclea?
questions.explanation: In Sidney's Arcadia, Basilius is the Duke of Arcadia, married to Gynecia and father of the princesses Pamela and Philoclea; Samuel Richardson later borrowed the name of his 1740 heroine Pamela from Sidney's romance.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which University Wit wrote the 1579 critical pamphlet A Defence of Poetry, Music, and Stage Plays as an immediate reply to Stephen Gosson's The School of Abuse?
questions.explanation: Before Sir Philip Sidney's An Apology for Poetry was printed in 1595, the Oxford-educated University Wit Thomas Lodge wrote A Defence of Poetry, Music, and Stage Plays (1579) in direct reply to Stephen Gosson's The School of Abuse.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which 1588 prose pastoral romance by Robert Greene—subtitled The Triumph of Time—served as the primary plot source for William Shakespeare's late romance The Winter's Tale?
questions.explanation: Robert Greene's prose romance Pandosto: The Triumph of Time (1588), dedicated to George Clifford, Earl of Cumberland, provided the main plot for Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which 1592 satirical prose pamphlet by Thomas Nashe takes the form of a penniless writer's comic petition to the Devil and satirizes contemporary London society through the Seven Deadly Sins?
options: Pierce Penilesse, His Supplication to the Divell
The Unfortunate Traveller, or The Life of Jack Wilton
questions.explanation: Thomas Nashe's Pierce Penilesse, His Supplication to the Divell (1592), a satire structured around the Seven Deadly Sins, was his most popular pamphlet alongside his picaresque novel The Unfortunate Traveller (1594).
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which Elizabethan critic published A Discourse of English Poetrie in 1586, surveying English poets from Chaucer to Spenser and advocating classical quantitative metres?
questions.explanation: William Webbe published A Discourse of English Poetrie in 1586, one of the earliest systematic Elizabethan treatises attempting to classify English poets and analyse quantitative and rhyming metres.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which Elizabethan critic is the author of the comprehensive three-book treatise The Arte of English Poesie, published in 1589?
questions.explanation: George Puttenham's The Arte of English Poesie (1589) is the most systematic Elizabethan critical handbook on the history of poetry, metrical proportion, and rhetorical figures.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which Elizabethan poet and critic wrote A Defence of Ryme (1602/1603) in reply to Thomas Campion's Observations in the Art of English Poesie (1602)?
questions.explanation: When Thomas Campion attacked rhyme in Observations in the Art of English Poesie (1602), Samuel Daniel settled the Elizabethan metre controversy with his critical treatise A Defence of Ryme (1602/1603).
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which Elizabethan theologian wrote the monumental defence of the Church of England, Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (First Four Books, 1594; Book V, 1597)?
questions.explanation: Richard Hooker (1554–1600) wrote Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (1594–1597), a masterpiece of stately, periodic Elizabethan theological and political prose defending the Anglican settlement against Puritan attacks.
questions.src: user-supplied: Upkar's UGC NET/JRF/SET English

questions.question:
Which of the following four specific charges against poetry—levelled by Stephen Gosson in The School of Abuse (1579)—does Sir Philip Sidney systematically refute in An Apology for Poetry?
(A) That there are many more fruitful branches of knowledge in which a man might better spend his time.
(B) That poetry is the 'mother of lies' and the 'nurse of abuse' infecting readers with pestilent desires.
(C) That Plato banished poets from his ideal Commonwealth in the Republic.
(D) That English poetry should only be written in Anglo-Saxon alliterative metre without any classical learning.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry, Sidney explicitly lists and refutes Gosson's four objections: (1) that other knowledge is more fruitful, (2) that poetry is the mother of lies, (3) that it is the nurse of abuse, and (4) that Plato banished poets. Statement (D) is false.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: What is the interlocking rhyme scheme of the fourteen-line Spenserian sonnet, created by Edmund Spenser for his 1595 sequence Amoretti?
questions.explanation: The Spenserian sonnet (used in Spenser's Amoretti, 1595) links its three quatrains by repeating the second rhyme of each quatrain as the first rhyme of the next, followed by a couplet: abab bcbc cdcd ee.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Glossary of Poetic Terms

questions.question: Which fellow dramatist coined the tribute 'Marlowe's mighty line' in his 1623 First Folio poem to describe the resonant blank verse of Christopher Marlowe?
questions.explanation: In his commendatory poem prefixed to Shakespeare's First Folio (1623), Ben Jonson coined the famous phrase 'Marlowe's mighty line' to characterize the power and grandeur of Marlowe's tragic blank verse.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which Roman Stoic philosopher and tragedian's blood-and-revenge plays—featuring ghosts, five acts, and declamatory speeches—served as the classical model for Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy and Elizabethan tragedy of blood?
questions.explanation: The Latin tragedies of Seneca inspired the Elizabethan 'tragedy of blood' (revenge tragedy), supplying conventions such as the vengeful ghost, five-act division, stichomythia, and sensational onstage bloodshed.
questions.src: user-supplied: Easy Handbook for NET English Literature

questions.question: Which modern literary scholar coined the critical term 'Revenge Tragedy' in 1900 to classify plays such as Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy and Shakespeare's Hamlet?
questions.explanation: The critical label 'Revenge Tragedy' was first introduced by the American scholar A. H. Thorndike in 1900 in his study of the relations of Hamlet to contemporary revenge plays.
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: What scholarly name is given to the lost pre-Shakespearean play about the Prince of Denmark (alluded to by Thomas Nashe in 1589 in his Preface to Greene's Menaphon) that is generally attributed to Thomas Kyd?
questions.explanation: Scholars call the lost earlier Elizabethan Hamlet play (first mentioned by Thomas Nashe in 1589 in his preface to Robert Greene's Menaphon and usually attributed to Thomas Kyd) the 'Ur-Hamlet' (from the German prefix Ur-, meaning 'primordial' or 'original').
questions.src: user-supplied: World Literature in Your Fist (3rd edn)

questions.question: Which of the following is the defining stylistic feature of John Lyly's 'Euphuism'?
options: Terse, unadorned scientific aphorisms stripped of all figures of speech
Balanced antithesis reinforced by transverse alliteration and allusions to unnatural natural history
Unrhymed iambic pentameter verse paragraphs with frequent enjambment
Rustic Northern dialect modelled on medieval Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse
questions.explanation: Euphuism, inaugurated in Lyly's Euphues (1578), is marked by symmetrical antithesis ('contrary expressions'), persistent alliteration, rhetorical questions, and similes drawn from classical myth and Pliny's natural history.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question: Which narrative genre—inaugurated in English prose by Thomas Nashe's The Unfortunate Traveller, or The Life of Jack Wilton (1594)—follows the episodic adventures of a clever rogue or page living by his wits?
questions.explanation: Thomas Nashe's The Unfortunate Traveller, or The Life of Jack Wilton (1594) is the earliest picaresque novel in English, recounting the episodic continental adventures of the roguish page Jack Wilton.
questions.src: user-supplied: Easy Handbook for NET English Literature

questions.question: Which 1576 blank-verse work by George Gascoigne is recognized in literary history as the first regular verse satire in English?
questions.explanation: George Gascoigne's The Steele Glas (1576), written in blank verse and contrasting the honest old-fashioned steel mirror with the flattering crystal glass of modern corruption, is the first regular verse satire in English.
questions.src: user-supplied: Easy Handbook for NET English Literature

questions.question: From which 1587 Tudor historical work did William Shakespeare (as well as Christopher Marlowe for Edward II) draw the primary material for his English history plays?
options: Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland
Sir Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's Lives
Richard Hakluyt's The Principal Navigations of the English Nation
questions.explanation: Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1577; 2nd edition 1587) served as the primary historical source for Shakespeare's English history plays (as well as Macbeth, King Lear, and Cymbeline) and Marlowe's Edward II.
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature

questions.question:
Match List I (Critical Treatise of the Elizabethan Age) with List II (Author):

List I (Critical Treatise)
(A) The School of Abuse (1579)
(B) A Discourse of English Poetrie (1586)
(C) The Arte of English Poesie (1589)
(D) A Defence of Ryme (1602/1603)

List II (Author)
(I) William Webbe
(II) Stephen Gosson
(III) Samuel Daniel
(IV) George Puttenham
questions.explanation: Stephen Gosson wrote The School of Abuse in 1579 (A-II); William Webbe wrote A Discourse of English Poetrie in 1586 (B-I); George Puttenham wrote The Arte of English Poesie in 1589 (C-IV); and Samuel Daniel wrote A Defence of Ryme in 1602/1603 (D-III).
questions.src: user-supplied: A Brief History of British Literature
